Moz Farooque ACCA

^IXIC

This article first appeared on GuruFocus.

U.S. stocks gave up an early lift Friday after a softer-than-expected producer price report offered only brief relief. Wholesale prices rose 0.3% in October, below the 0.4% economists expected, but annual inflation accelerated to 6.5%, its highest since November 2022. That leaves the Federal Reserve under pressure to raise rates in December, even as investors grapple with renewed weakness in technology shares.

Is QQQ fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

S&P 500 futures were up 0.37% at 8:39 a.m. ET, according to TipRanks. By 10:08 a.m., the index was down 0.7%, the Nasdaq Composite had fallen 1.1% and the Dow was off 0.2%, Reuters reported. Nvidia (NVDA) pared its premarket gains as investors assessed the fallout from co-founder Jensen Huang's resignation.

September's producer price increase was revised up to 1.4%, making October's slowdown more pronounced. Goods prices rose 0.5%, led by food and basic organic chemicals, while services prices climbed 0.2% for a fifth consecutive monthly increase. The report followed a hotter-than-expected consumer inflation reading earlier in the week. Reuters reported that markets were weighing a quarter-point December hike while leaving room for a half-point move.

Investors Takeaway

The two-year Treasury yield can show whether the softer monthly reading changes expectations for the Fed's Dec. 89 meeting. November's consumer price report is due Dec. 10, a day after the decision, making the Fed's updated rate projections particularly important for judging whether another hike could follow in January.

For tech stocks, Nvidia's Nov. 17 earnings report is a separate test. Strong data center guidance could help stabilize chip shares. Weaker guidance alongside rising yields would leave the Nasdaq exposed to both lower earnings expectations and higher borrowing costs.

title: QQQ Is in a Correction (Down 10%). Should You Buy More of This Popular Tech ETF?

QQQ Is in a Correction (Down 10%). Should You Buy More of This Popular Tech ETF?
Ben Gran, The Motley Fool
Fri, November 13, 2026 at 6:01 AM PST 5 min read
QQQ
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The years-long stock market boom powered by artificial intelligence (AI) stocks seems to be at a crossroads. Investors are worried about rising levels of AI company debt, voter backlash against data centers, and concerns that AI tools won't deliver significant gains in productivity.

Doubts about the AI trade are showing up in one of the most important tech exchange-traded funds (ETFs) that tracks the Nasdaq-100 index. The Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ: QQQ) has lost about 11.2% (as of Nov. 10) since its record high on Oct. 6. Tech stocks are officially in a "correction" (a broad decline of 10% or more). Could this AI sell-off go further and reach a bear market?

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Let's look at whether you should buy QQQ now after a 10% (or more) decline in share prices -- and why it depends on what you believe will happen next with AI stocks.

Image source: Getty Images.
What's driving the decline in AI stocks? Doubts.

The AI boom has been fueled by positive emotions about the future: enthusiasm, optimism, hope. Many AI investors believe that AI companies are building a revolutionary technology that could be more important to the economy than the internet, the telephone, or perhaps electricity. If you believe AI will make everyone richer -- and its early investors especially rich -- you want to get in on the ground floor.

But more recently, negative emotions about AI have been creeping in: worry, fear, doubt. Many investors are questioning the high costs of the AI build-out. They worry that AI companies are spending too much, too rapidly, on developing technology that hasn't clearly demonstrated enough value to the economy. They're skeptical that the hundreds of billions of dollars of AI capital expenditures (capex) will pay off anytime soon.

Some major tech stocks have gone through big share price declines as more of those companies' free cash flow gets devoted to AI capex. Major tech names at the center of the AI trade, like Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG)(NASDAQ: GOOGL), Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA), and Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA), have had double-digit declines in their share prices in the past six months. As of Nov. 10, Alphabet is down about 26.3%, Nvidia is down about 23.1%, and Tesla is down about 14.7% in that time frame. These stocks are three of the 10 largest holdings in QQQ as of Nov. 9.

Now put your own balance next to it. In a $2 million portfolio held in an S&P 500 fund, that is about $123,000 of Nvidia and about $740,000 in ten holdings. Few statements ever show that sum. The fund's name says 500, the balance is a single line, and no one asks you each year whether the share at the top still suits you. This week showed what one person's news can do: Nvidia fell 4.3% on Thursday, when Jensen Huang resigned as CEO, and is down 11.0% since the Nov 6 close, while the S&P 500 fund rose 3.0%.

That $123,000 was sized by the index, not by you. For families with seven figures invested, the same names often reappear in tech and retirement funds. Do you know your total? A Trefis partner firm can add it up with you in a free 30-minute call.

Less concentration is not automatically safer, either. In 2008 the equal-weight fund fell 40.1%, more than the S&P 500 fund's 36.8%. No path wins every decade. Each answers a different purpose.

What Would A Number On Purpose Look Like?

A ceiling. Pick a share for the top 7-10 names across everything you own, and write it down.

A blend. Pair a size-weighted core with an equal-weight or dividend-growth sleeve, if you want the number lower.

A rule, not a headline. Check twice a year; trim only when you cross the line.

title: Warren Buffett’s 1979 Warning May Be the Perfect Lesson for Today’s AI Boom, Says Howard Marks: ‘Uncertainty Actually is the Friend’
detail:
Warren Buffett’s 1979 Warning May Be the Perfect Lesson for Today’s AI Boom, Says Howard Marks: ‘Uncertainty Actually is the Friend’
Warren Buffett (Credit: Image via Shutterstock)
Rishabh Mishra
Fri, November 13, 2026 at 4:30 AM PST 5 min read
QQQ
Trade QQQ on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Benzinga and Yahoo Finance LLC may earn commission or revenue on some items through the links below.

Oaktree Capital Management co-founder Howard Marks used a 1979 statement by veteran investor Warren Buffett to advise clients on navigating the artificial intelligence sector in the current market.

A Lesson in Uncertainty

In a memo titled "A Layman Thinks About AI," Marks stated that investors should not abstain from the AI industry despite its unpredictability. In his memo, Marks concluded by citing a quote from Warren Buffett published in Forbes magazine on Aug. 6, 1979.

Don't Miss:

A single bad hire can set a startup back years. Here are the 5 hires founders most often misjudge — and why

Still Learning the Market? These 50 Must-Know Terms Can Help You Catch Up Fast

Buffett's quote advises investors against waiting for a "cheery consensus" because the future is never clear. Marks emphasized Buffett's statement that "uncertainty actually is the friend of the buyer of long-term values." Marks designated this 1979 warning as the "perfect ending for a memo on AI."

Assessing Unpredictability

Marks described AI as the "most consequential and least predictable development for investors in at least a generation." He noted that investors in AI must correctly forecast technological evolution, compute demand, and financing availability.

To quantify the uncertainty, Marks asked Anthropic's Claude to rate AI's predictability on a scale of one to 10. The model assigned AI an overall score of three, while giving the economic outcomes investors care about, including profitability, timing and which companies capture the gains, a score of just two.

Marks concluded that determining whether the trillions of dollars invested in AI infrastructure will generate adequate returns is presently a "matter of faith."

Trending: Avoid the #1 Investing Mistake: How Your 'Safe' Holdings Could Be Costing You Big Time

The Recommended Strategy

Despite the sector's risks, Marks advised his clients that the correct response is not investment paralysis. Instead, Marks recommended that market participants approach the sector with "calibrated humility regarding strategy selection, position sizing, and risk-taking."

He emphasized the necessity of a "willingness to act in the presence of uncertainty." Marks warned that investors must accept they do not possess complete knowledge, stating that the AI sector is certain to produce surprises.

How Has the Stock Market and AI-linked ETFs Performed?

The S&P 500 index has advanced 11.3% year-to-date. Similarly, the Nasdaq Composite index was up 9.57%, and the Dow Jones gained 9.2% YTD.

Goldman Sachs strategists said hyperscalers are trading well below their historical valuations following a selloff in major technology stocks.

The bank forecasts S&P 500 EPS growth to slow to 11% in 2027 from 36% in 2026.

Goldman favors U.S. and Japanese equities but is 'Underweight' on Europe.

Goldman Sachs strategists led by Peter Oppenheimer reportedly see technology stocks, particularly artificial intelligence (AI) hyperscalers, as relatively defensive investments after a recent selloff pushed their valuations below historical levels.

The firm expects the S&P 500 to climb about 14% to 8,700 points over the next 12 months, despite forecasting a sharp slowdown in corporate earnings growth, Bloomberg reported on Friday. Goldman is overweight U.S. and Japanese equities heading into 2027.

At the time of writing, Nasdaq 100 futures were marginally lower, signaling a muted opening for technology stocks. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ), which tracks the Nasdaq 100, remained in 'bullish' territory.

See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox

Hyperscalers Seen As Relatively Defensive

The Nasdaq-100 has fallen over 9% from its early October peak amid concerns about AI infrastructure spending and the controversy surrounding Nvidia (NVDA) former CEO Jensen Huang.

Over the past month, META shares have declined about 18%, GOOG stock has fallen nearly 16%, ORCL stock has shed over 11%, and MSFT stock has slipped nearly 4%. Amazon (AMZN) has bucked the trend, gaining more than 3% over the same period.

Goldman strategists said the decline has left hyperscalers trading "well below" their historical valuations. "We see Technology — and the Hyperscalers in particular — as relatively defensive," they said as per the note cited by the publication.

They acknowledged that the largest companies have turned cash-flow negative but said their broader balance-sheet measures, including net debt relative to equity, remain healthy.

Sharp Slowdown Seen In Earnings Growth

Goldman forecasts S&P 500 earnings-per-share (EPS) growth will slow to 11% in 2027 from 36% in 2026. For Europe's Stoxx 600 index, it expects growth to ease to 7% from 18%.

The strategists expect investors to increasingly favor businesses that can sustain growth as earnings expansion becomes less widespread, the publication said. They identified opportunities in long-duration growth companies, which they expect to become more valuable as growth rates slow.

What does SNPS do?

Synopsys is the world's largest supplier of electronic design automation (EDA) software, the tools engineers use to design and verify semiconductor chips, and a leading provider of semiconductor IP, pre-designed circuit blocks including interface, foundation, and processor IP that customers license rather than build.

Synopsys reported trailing-12-month revenue of $9.41 billion, up 20.9% over one year, with a 62.9% gross margin and an 11.4% net margin. It trades at a P/E of 81.73, P/B of 2.85 and P/S of 9.38, with a market cap of $88.7 billion. Its GF Score is 96 and GF Value is $667.18 versus a price of $462.69, and the stock is down 1.5% year to date.
